analogy.p: Think of an ecosystem as a tower built from many different kinds of blocks. If the tower is built from many types of block, each supporting its neighbours, removing a few blocks does not make it fall, because others can take the load. If the tower is built from one kind of block stacked in a single column, removing just one block can topple the whole tower. High biodiversity is the wide, varied tower; a monoculture is the single column. The analogy breaks down because species are living and interact in complex ways, such as eating each other, whereas blocks simply rest on each other.

bullets: A **species** is a group of organisms that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring; biodiversity counts the number of different species.
Biodiversity can be described for a small area (a pond, a hedgerow) or for the whole planet.
Tropical rainforests and coral reefs are examples of areas of very high biodiversity.
Intensively farmed fields, lawns and city centres have low biodiversity because few species live there.
Biodiversity is measured by sampling (quadrats, transects, pitfall traps, nets) and counting the number of species, not just the number of individuals.
A large number of individuals of one species does not mean high biodiversity: variety of species is what counts.
Biodiversity is threatened by human activity and is a key theme in the ecology topic.
core.p: **Biodiversity** is the variety of all the different species of organisms on Earth, or within an ecosystem. It includes the number of different species and, in a wider sense, the genetic variety within each species and the range of habitats. A habitat such as a rainforest or coral reef has high biodiversity, while a field of wheat grown as a single crop has very low biodiversity. The AQA specification wording to remember is that biodiversity is 'the variety of all the different species of organisms on earth, or within an ecosystem'.

bullets: More species means more **alternative food sources**, so predators can switch prey if one species becomes scarce.
Plants provide **shelter** and nest sites; a variety of plants supports a variety of animals.
Species help to maintain the **physical environment**: for example, trees prevent soil erosion and regulate water flow, and decomposers return minerals to the soil.
A **monoculture** (one crop grown over a large area) is vulnerable: a single disease or pest can destroy the whole crop.
The future of the human species relies on maintaining a good level of biodiversity because humans depend on other species for food, medicines, materials and clean air and water.
Many species are the source of new drugs and foods; extinct species are lost forever, along with their potential uses.
In exam answers, state both ideas: 'reduces dependence of one species on another' and 'stability of the ecosystem'.
core.h: Why high biodiversity matters for stable ecosystems
core.p: A high level of biodiversity **ensures the stability of ecosystems by reducing the dependence of one species on another for food, shelter and the maintenance of the physical environment**. In an ecosystem with many species, there are many food chains linked in complex food webs, so if one species declines, others can take its place as food or fill its role. In an ecosystem with few species, the loss of one species can cause a collapse of the whole system. This is why scientists and governments try to protect biodiversity.

bullets: **Rapid growth in the human population** means more demand for resources such as food, fuel, water and land.
**An increase in the standard of living** means more goods are made and more waste is produced per person, for example electronics, packaging, cars.
Humans use resources faster than they are replaced, which is not **sustainable** for many resources.
More waste means more pollution unless it is dealt with properly.
More people need more land for building, farming, quarrying and dumping waste.
If not managed, the combined effect is to reduce the land and habitats available to other species and reduce biodiversity.
Many of the effects can be reduced by recycling, reducing waste, and using sustainable methods (see maintaining biodiversity).
core.p: The human population has been growing rapidly, and the standard of living has also been rising in many countries. Both factors increase the use of resources and the production of waste. More people need more food, water, energy, housing and goods, and as living standards rise, each person typically consumes more and throws away more. This pressure on the environment is the driver behind most of the effects on biodiversity covered in this topic.

bullets: **Water pollution** can be caused by sewage, fertiliser and toxic chemicals, for example from factories.
**Air pollution** can be caused by smoke and acidic gases, such as sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen produced by burning fossil fuels.
**Land pollution** can be caused by landfill and toxic chemicals, for example household waste buried in the ground, or chemicals such as pesticides and herbicides.
Pollution can kill plants and animals directly, or make habitats unsuitable, which reduces biodiversity.
Proper waste treatment, such as sewage treatment, recycling and controlled disposal, limits the damage.
Waste produced by modern living includes household rubbish, industrial waste, sewage and agricultural waste.
Some pollutants stay in the environment for a long time; others, like acidic gases, travel long distances before causing harm.
core.p: If waste is not handled properly, it can **pollute the water, the air and the land**. Pollution is the release of harmful substances into the environment. Pollution kills plants and animals, which can reduce biodiversity. The specification expects you to link each type of pollution to its source. Waste management means controlling and treating waste so that it does not damage ecosystems.

bullets: **Building** houses, roads and factories covers natural habitat with concrete and tarmac.
**Quarrying** removes soil, rocks and vegetation to extract materials such as stone and clay.
**Farming** replaces diverse natural vegetation with a few crops or grazing animals; hedgerows may be removed to make fields larger.
**Dumping waste** (landfill) covers land and can pollute it with toxic substances.
Each activity reduces the area of habitat, so populations of wild species fall and some may become extinct.
Fragmentation of habitats by roads and fields can isolate populations, which makes them more vulnerable.
Land use is a trade-off: humans need homes and food, but biodiversity is lost.
core.h: Land use: reducing the land available to wildlife
core.p: Humans reduce the amount of land available for other animals and plants by **building, quarrying, farming and dumping waste**. As natural habitats are replaced by towns, roads, fields and quarries, the species that lived there lose their food, shelter and breeding sites. Habitat destruction is one of the main causes of species loss. This is a very common 'explain' question: give the four activities and link each to loss of habitat and reduced biodiversity.

bullets: Peat forms in **waterlogged, acidic conditions** where decomposers cannot work well, so dead plants do not fully decay.
Peat bogs are home to specialised species that cannot live elsewhere, such as sphagnum moss and some insects and birds.
Digging up peat for garden compost **destroys the habitat** and so reduces biodiversity.
Peat takes thousands of years to form so it is effectively **non-renewable** on human timescales.
When peat is removed, it decays or is burned, which releases **carbon dioxide**, a greenhouse gas.
Using peat-free compost made from other materials, and protecting peat bogs, reduces the harm.
Link: this is an example of the carbon cycle being disturbed because a carbon store is being released.
core.p: Peat is a natural store of carbon formed over thousands of years from partly decayed plants in waterlogged conditions. Peat bogs are a rare habitat with specialised species. The specification points out that destruction of **peat bogs and other areas of peat to produce garden compost** reduces the area of this habitat and so reduces biodiversity. In addition, the **decay or burning of the peat releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere**, which adds to the greenhouse effect and global warming.

bullets: Reasons: land for **cattle** (beef production) and **rice fields** (rice paddies produce methane), and for growing crops to make **biofuels**.
Trees are removed so there is **less photosynthesis**, so less carbon dioxide is removed from the atmosphere.
If trees are burned or decay, **carbon dioxide** is released.
Cattle and rice fields release **methane**, another greenhouse gas.
The loss of tree habitat leads to **extinction** of species and reduced biodiversity.
Loss of trees can also lead to soil erosion and changes in rainfall patterns.
Link to the later notes on global warming, deforestation and maintaining biodiversity.
core.p: Large-scale **deforestation** (removal of forests) in tropical areas has occurred to provide land for **cattle and rice fields** and to grow **crops for biofuels**. Deforestation destroys the habitat of huge numbers of species, and tropical forests are some of the most biodiverse places on Earth. It also affects the carbon cycle and the climate. The detail of the effects on global warming is covered in the global warming topic, but you should know the reasons for clearing the forests and the effect on biodiversity.

bullets: Always give the **chain of cause and effect**, not just the final result.
Habitat loss reduces food, shelter and breeding sites for wild species.
Pollution can kill organisms directly or make habitats unsuitable.
Lower biodiversity makes ecosystems less stable.
Some humans actions can increase biodiversity, such as creating nature reserves, planting hedgerows and reintroducing species (see maintaining biodiversity).
A balanced answer might mention that some of these activities are necessary for human needs.
Humans also depend on healthy ecosystems, so reducing biodiversity can harm people in the long run.
core.h: Effects of human activity on biodiversity: linking the ideas
core.p: Putting the content together, human activity reduces biodiversity in two main ways: by destroying or reducing habitat (land use and deforestation) and by polluting the environment (water, air and land). The cause of both is the growth in population and the rise in the standard of living. Examiners expect a chain of reasoning: more people and higher standard of living -> more waste and use of land -> pollution and habitat loss -> death of organisms and fewer species -> reduced biodiversity.

bullets: Describe a trend using **numbers from the graph**, for example 'species fell from 40 to 12 between 1990 and 2020'.
Correlation does not prove cause: other factors might also have changed.
Compare a polluted site and a clean site using the number of species or an indicator species.
Be aware that sample size and sampling method affect the reliability of the data.
Percentage change = (change / original) x 100, a common calculation.
Link the data to the explanation in the specification: pollution, habitat loss, or deforestation.
Use cautious language such as 'this suggests' when the data cannot prove a cause.
core.h: Interpreting data on biodiversity and human impact
core.p: You may be asked to analyse data such as graphs of species numbers over time, tables comparing sites with different land uses, or maps showing pollution. The skills are to describe the trend with figures, link the change to a human activity, and avoid claiming more than the data shows. Always look for the units, the time scale and whether the data show a correlation or prove a cause.

bullets: **Economic**: jobs and money from farming, quarrying or logging versus the cost of ecosystem damage.
**Social**: housing and food for a growing population versus loss of natural spaces.
**Environmental**: loss of biodiversity, increased carbon dioxide, pollution.
Sustainable approaches meet current needs without damaging the ability of future generations to meet theirs.
Reducing, reusing and recycling waste reduces both pollution and the need for landfill.
Protecting peat bogs and forests keeps carbon stored and preserves habitats.
Evaluation answers should reach a conclusion, for example by saying which action has the greatest benefit and why.
core.p: Some questions ask you to evaluate how humans can meet their needs while protecting biodiversity. This means weighing the economic, social and environmental factors. For example, farmers need to make a living, builders need land and consumers want cheap products, but protecting biodiversity helps ensure long-term food, medicine and ecosystem services. Good answers give both sides and finish with a justified judgement.

bullets: **Communities and interdependence (4.7.1)**: loss of one species affects others in the food web.
**Biomass transfers (4.7.2, triple)**: the number of trophic levels is limited, so top predators are especially vulnerable to habitat loss.
**Global warming and deforestation (4.7.3)**: land use and peat destruction release carbon dioxide.
**Maintaining biodiversity (4.7.3)**: how humans can reduce the negative effects.
**Carbon cycle (4.7.2)**: burning and decay of peat and forests release carbon dioxide.
**Evolution and extinction (4.6)**: habitat loss and pollution are causes of extinction.
**Required practical (quadrats and transects)**: the sampling methods used to measure biodiversity.
core.p: Human impact on biodiversity brings together much of ecology and links to other parts of the course. It follows on from interdependence in communities and connects to the carbon cycle, global warming, maintaining biodiversity, food security and evolution/extinction.

exam: **Define (1 mark)** biodiversity: 'the variety of all the different species of organisms on Earth, or within an ecosystem'.
**State (1-2 marks)** ways humans reduce land for wildlife: building, quarrying, farming and dumping waste. Give as many as the marks.
**Explain (2 marks)** why biodiversity is important: reduces dependence of one species on another for food, shelter and maintaining the physical environment, so ecosystems are stable.
**Name the pollutant and the area**: water (sewage, fertiliser, toxic chemicals), air (smoke, acidic gases), land (landfill, toxic chemicals). Match them correctly.
**Explain (3-4 marks)** how a growing population reduces biodiversity: increases use of resources and waste, more pollution and land used, so organisms die or lose habitat, so fewer species.
**Peat questions**: say it destroys a habitat AND releases carbon dioxide when it decays or burns.
**Deforestation questions**: give a reason (cattle, rice fields, biofuel crops) and an effect (habitat loss, extra carbon dioxide, methane).
**6-mark evaluate**: give benefits of the human activity, the harm to biodiversity, link to the data, and reach a conclusion with a reason.
**Graph/data**: quote figures with units, describe the trend, and state possible causes; use 'suggests' unless the data prove a cause.
Use the **linking words** 'so', 'which leads to', 'therefore' to show cause and effect; mark schemes reward the chain of reasoning.

mistakes.r: Biodiversity is the **variety of different species**, not the total number of individuals.
mistakes.w: Biodiversity means the number of animals in an area.

mistakes.r: Pollution **kills plants and animals**, which reduces biodiversity.
mistakes.w: Pollution just makes the area look dirty.

mistakes.r: Also by **building, quarrying, farming and dumping waste**, which reduce the land available, and by pollution.
mistakes.w: Humans reduce biodiversity by hunting only.

mistakes.r: Peat bogs are a **habitat**, and destroying them for garden compost reduces biodiversity and releases carbon dioxide.
mistakes.w: Peat is used for fuel only, so it is not a habitat.

mistakes.r: Deforestation destroys habitats, reduces carbon dioxide uptake and, when trees burn or decay, releases carbon dioxide.
mistakes.w: Deforestation just means fewer trees, so less oxygen.
Rice fields and cattle give out carbon dioxide only.

mistakes.r: High biodiversity helps ensure **stable ecosystems** and humans depend on it for food, medicines and a stable environment.
mistakes.w: Biodiversity matters only to wild animals.

mistakes.r: Fertiliser washed into water is a **water pollutant**.
mistakes.w: Fertiliser is always good for the environment because plants grow.

summary: AQA GCSE biology asks you to know that biodiversity is the variety of species and that high biodiversity keeps ecosystems stable, and to explain how a growing human population, waste and pollution of water, air and land, land use (building, quarrying, farming, dumping waste), peat destruction and large-scale deforestation reduce biodiversity. It matters because 4 to 6 mark cause-and-effect questions on human impact are common on Paper 2.

terms.d: The variety of all the different species of organisms on Earth, or within an ecosystem.
The interaction of a community of living organisms (biotic) with the non-living (abiotic) parts of their environment.
A group of organisms that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring.
The growing of a single crop over a large area, which has very low biodiversity.
When no individuals of a species remain alive.
The release of harmful substances into the environment.
Waste water and human waste that can pollute water if untreated.
Chemicals added to soil to provide minerals for plant growth, which can pollute water if washed off fields.
The burying of waste in the ground, which takes up land and can cause land pollution.
The large-scale removal of forests, for example to provide land for cattle, rice fields and biofuel crops.
Partly decayed plant material, formed in waterlogged conditions, that stores carbon.
The place where an organism lives.
Meeting the needs of the present without damaging the ability of future generations to meet their needs.
Fuel made from plant material, grown as a crop.
The level of wealth and comfort a person or population has, which affects how much they consume.

worked.ans: Full-mark model: As the population grows and living standards rise, more resources are used and more waste is produced. More land is taken for building, quarrying, farming and dumping waste, so habitats for wild plants and animals are lost. If waste is not handled properly it pollutes water, air and land and kills organisms. With habitats lost and organisms killed, fewer species survive, so biodiversity falls.
worked.q: Explain how the growth of the human population can reduce biodiversity. (4 marks)
steps: Mark 1: more people use more resources and produce more waste.
Mark 2: they need more land for building, quarrying, farming and dumping waste, which reduces the habitat available for other species.
Mark 3: waste can pollute water, air and land, which kills plants and animals.
Mark 4: so there are fewer species, so biodiversity is reduced.

worked.ans: The habitat is destroyed, reducing biodiversity, and the peat decays or burns, releasing carbon dioxide which adds to global warming.
worked.q: Peat is dug up from bogs to make garden compost. Explain two effects of this on the environment. (4 marks)
steps: Mark 1: peat bogs are a habitat, so digging them up destroys the habitat of specialised species.
Mark 3: peat is a store of carbon; when it is removed it decays or is burned.
Mark 4: this releases carbon dioxide, which increases global warming.

worked.q: A survey of a river found 24 species upstream of a farm and 9 species downstream. Calculate the percentage decrease in species and suggest a cause. (3 marks)
steps: Cause: fertiliser or sewage washed into the river from the farm pollutes the water and kills organisms.
